record.original_question: Given an arbitrary irreducible algebraic surface S, does there exist a rational map from S to P^3 that is birational onto its image and whose image has only isolated singularities?

evidence.quote: Problem 10 (Ciro Ciliberto) The following is a folklore problem, attributed to D. Mumford: Given an arbitrary irreducible algebraic surface S, is there a rational map S ￾￾ P3, birational onto its image ￾, with ￾ having only isolated singularities?

artifact.self_contained_problem: Work over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Let $S$ be an arbitrary irreducible projective algebraic surface. Does there exist a rational map $\varphi : S \dashrightarrow \mathbb{P}^3$ that is birational onto its image $\Sigma = \overline{\varphi(S)} \subset \mathbb{P}^3$, such that $\Sigma$ has only isolated singularities (i.e., the singular locus of $\Sigma$ is zero-dimensional)?
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a folklore problem attributed to D. Mumford, and is listed as an open problem. Web searches turned up no published resolution; standard projection arguments give birational maps to P^3 with ordinary (non-isolated, double curve) singularities, but achieving only isolated singularities for an arbitrary surface remains unresolved as far as can be verified.

status_evidence.title: Singularities of some projective rational surfaces — R. Piene
status_evidence.snippet: For most linear projections of a nonsingular surface to P^3, the induced map is finite and birational, with image having only ordinary singularities (double curve plus pinch points/triple points).
status_evidence.claim: Classical projection yields birational maps to P^3 with non-isolated (ordinary) singularities, not isolated ones, indicating that Mumford's stronger question is non-trivial.

status_evidence.title: Mumford, Topology of normal singularities of an algebraic surface
status_evidence.snippet: Mumford's classical work on isolated normal surface singularities.
status_evidence.claim: Background context for Mumford's interest in isolated surface singularities; no resolution of the folklore question is provided.
